identity.title: The Text Isn't the Destination
identity.description: Clicking a link takes you somewhere. That somewhere is never the word you clicked — it's named separately, in an attribute. This lesson builds the model that connects visible content to the resource it actually points at, and shows that links and images work the same way.

primaryCapability.statement: Explain how an attribute like href or src names a separate resource for the browser to retrieve, distinct from the visible text or image that activates it.

knows: Attributes configure a specific element instance
canDo: Read and construct simple attributes on an element
likelyMisconceptions: The clickable text of a link IS the destination
Images just "contain" their picture the way a paragraph contains its words

canDo: Explain that href names a destination separate from the link's visible text
Explain that src names a resource for the browser to fetch and display
Construct a link and an image that both correctly reference a resource

learning.targetMentalModel: A link's text and an image's alt text are what the learner sees. The attribute — href, src — is a separate, named pointer to the actual resource. Changing the visible text never changes the destination; only changing the attribute does. and both work this exact same way: attribute names the resource, browser retrieves it.

experience.startingState: The learner can configure an element with attributes but hasn't yet separated 'what you see' from 'what it points to'.
experience.narrativeContext: A link whose visible text doesn't match its real destination is used to force the distinction into view.
experience.primaryInteraction: Predicting a link's real destination, then constructing a correctly-referenced link and image.
experience.expectedOutcome: The learner treats visible content and its resource reference as two separate things by default.

activities.title: The Text Isn't the Destination
activities.instruction: A link that says one thing and does another.

content.title: The Text Isn't the Destination
content.hook: Read our blog The visible text says "Read our blog." Click it, and you land on the pricing page. Nothing about that is a bug — the browser is doing exactly what it was told.
content.context: What actually decides where a link goes was never the words you can see.
goals: Separate a resource reference from its visible content

content.title: Attribute Names the Resource
content.text: href is an attribute — you already know attributes configure an element. What it configures, specifically, is the destination: where the browser goes when this link is activated. The text between and is just what's clickable. It has no effect on where the click leads. uses the same idea with a different attribute: src names the image file for the browser to fetch and display. The alt text (a second attribute) is a description of that image, not the image itself — it's shown if the image fails to load, and read aloud by screen readers. In both cases the pattern is identical: attribute = pointer to a resource. Visible content = something else entirely.
content.keyTakeaway: href and src name a resource. The link text and alt text describe or represent it — they aren't it.

activities.title: Where Does It Actually Go?
activities.instruction: View our latest offers Where does clicking this link take you?

options.text: To /cart — that's what href names, regardless of the link text
To a page about "latest offers" — that's what the text says
Nowhere — the mismatch between text and href causes an error

hints.text: The browser only ever reads the attribute to decide where to go.
The link text is display content. It has no wiring to the navigation at all — only href does.

activities.title: Reference Both Resources
activities.instruction: Complete the markup: an linking to "/gallery" with the text "See more photos", and an whose src is "cover.jpg" and whose alt is "Trail overlook at sunrise".

content.solutionCode: See more photos

testCases.description: The image's alt is "Trail overlook at sunrise"

hints.text: Two separate attributes on <a>? No — just one, href, plus the text it already has.
needs two attributes: src for the file, alt for the description.
See more photos\n

content.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why doesn't changing a link's text also change where it goes?" Answer them, using href and the actual resource it names.
guidelines: Say what the visible text's actual job is, if not navigation

content.title: What You Can Do Now
takeaways: href names a link's real destination — separate from, and unaffected by, the link's visible text.
src names an image's actual file — separate from, and unaffected by, its alt text.
The pattern is the same across elements: attribute names the resource, visible content is something else.
nextSteps: Next: modeling sequential and tabular data with the right HTML structure.

requirements: meaningful alt text is itself part of this lesson's subject matter
